templates.name: Main idea, informational study report (incl. explainer and scholar-argument passages)

items.passage: Leafcutter bees typically build their nests from cut leaves and petals, though urban bees in Toronto, Canada, had been documented building some nest cells from plastic-bag scraps. Then, while checking wooden trap nests on a seed farm in San Juan, Argentina, researcher Mariana Allasino and her team discovered a leafcutter nest made entirely of plastic. Its three brood cells were built from two different plastics, one resembling a blue shopping bag. Allasino’s team sees the nest as evidence of bees’ flexibility in responding to environments altered by human activity.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Leafcutter bees in Argentina build their nests from different materials than leafcutter bees in Canada do.
The discovery of a nest made only of plastic suggests that bees can adapt to environments that people have changed.
Bees that use plastic to build their nests produce fewer young than bees that use leaves and petals.
Researchers placed plastic in trap nests to find out whether leafcutter bees would use it instead of leaves.
items.explanation: The text describes Allasino’s team finding a leafcutter nest built entirely of plastic and ends with the researchers’ view that it shows bees’ flexibility in responding to human-altered environments. Choice B states that finding and what the researchers take it to mean.

A.why_wrong: The text says bees in Toronto used some plastic and one nest in Argentina was all plastic; it does not say leafcutter bees in the two countries generally use different materials.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how many young the bees in plastic nests produce compared with other bees.

D.why_wrong: The researchers were monitoring wooden trap nests and found the plastic nest; nothing says they supplied plastic to test the bees.

sources.what: Crossref record of the Allasino note: authors Mariana L. Allasino, Hugo J. Marrero, Jimena Dorado, Juan Pablo Torretta (Apidologie 2019)

Allasino, Marrero, Torretta and Dorado 2019, Apidologie 50(2):230-233, “Scientific note: first global report of a bee nest built only with plastic”: Megachile sp. nest made entirely of plastic found in a trap nest on a seed-producing farm; first worldwide record of plastic used in the total construction of a bee nest; species survival depends on ability to adapt to new conditions

Coverage: Mariana Allasino led the team (INTA); San Juan, Argentina; wooden trap nests; three cells of two kinds of plastic, one like a blue shopping bag; researchers see adaptation to human-altered environments

Coverage (Spanish): seed-production field in San Juan province, more than 60 trap nests of wood, three cells, two types of plastic; Torretta frames the behavior as flexibility in response to environmental change
MacIvor and Moore 2013, Ecosphere 4(12):155: Megachile rotundata in Toronto built brood cells with cut pieces of polyethylene plastic bags; keywords include Toronto and urban environment
DOI of the Allasino note

items.notes: New subject (replaces the viral elephant-names study). The builder was a Megachile (leafcutter) bee whose species was not confirmed, so the passage says only “a leafcutter nest.” Allasino works at INTA (Argentina’s National Agricultural Technology Institute); the passage calls her “researcher.”

fixes: Simplified prose made dense on purpose (“typically construct”, “observed incorporating”, “monitoring”, “assembled”) to bring the easy tier closer to official density
Toronto clause now follows the source (bees built some nest cells from plastic-bag scraps, MacIvor and Moore 2013)
Closing sentence no longer uses the stock “The researchers regard” frame repeated across items

items.rewrite: New subject (all-plastic leafcutter bee nest in San Juan, Argentina, Allasino et al. 2019) replacing the viral elephant-names study; key no longer uses the 'Research suggests' frame; new distractor set without the overgeneralized and 'model unable' tells.

items.passage: Nine thousand years ago, a ridge of dry land now submerged beneath Lake Huron connected present-day Michigan and Ontario. On this ridge, archaeologists John O’Shea and Ashley Lemke used sonar to identify Drop 45, a lane of two parallel stone alignments with three built-in hunting blinds; given its orientation, it could have intercepted caribou only during their northwestward spring migration. Operating such a structure would have required a large cooperating group. The simpler V-shaped blinds nearby, aimed at the autumn migration, could have been run by small family groups, a contrast O’Shea and Lemke attribute to distinct seasonal hunting strategies.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Hunters on the ridge abandoned V-shaped blinds for larger structures such as Drop 45 after caribou stopped migrating there in autumn.
Because caribou crossed the ridge in greater numbers in spring, hunters there concentrated their efforts on the spring migration.
Remains on the ridge suggest that its ancient hunters organized caribou hunts differently depending on the season.
Drop 45 shows that small family groups built elaborate stone structures to hunt caribou in both spring and autumn.
items.explanation: The text sets Drop 45, a spring structure that needed a large cooperating group, beside the nearby autumn blinds that small family groups could run, and it ends by saying the researchers attribute the contrast to distinct seasonal hunting strategies. Choice C joins these points: the hunters organized their hunts differently by season.

A.why_wrong: The text presents the two kinds of structures as serving different seasons at the same place; it never says one replaced the other or that caribou stopped migrating in autumn.

B.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how many caribou crossed in each season, and it does not say hunters favored the spring migration; it describes structures for both seasons.

D.why_wrong: The text links small family groups to the simpler autumn blinds and says the elaborate Drop 45 required a large cooperating group used in spring, so it does not show small groups building elaborate structures for both seasons.

sources.what: O’Shea, Lemke et al. 2014, PNAS 111(19):6911-6915: 9,000-year-old Drop 45 Drive Lane on the Alpena-Amberley Ridge, a dry corridor from northeast Michigan to southern Ontario now under Lake Huron; found by side-scan and multibeam sonar; two parallel lines of stones with three circular hunting blinds; effective only for animals moving northwest in the spring migration; V-shaped blinds upslope oriented to intercept animals moving southeast in autumn; small blinds operable by very small family groups, complex lanes needing larger cooperating groups; distinctly different seasonal strategies
DOI of the paper

items.notes: New subject (replaces the plant-sounds study). The main idea is spread over the last three sentences (structure, group size, contrast), as in the medium models. O’Shea and Lemke are the first two authors (University of Michigan Museum of Anthropological Archaeology); the other authors are folded into the pair.

fixes: Removed the participial method opener (“Surveying the ridge with sonar, ...”) that recurred in four items
Fixed the ambiguous “which could have intercepted” (it modified the blinds, not Drop 45): now “oriented so that it could have intercepted caribou only during their northwestward spring migration”
Varied the stock “the researchers attribute” closer

items.rewrite: New subject (submerged caribou hunting structures under Lake Huron, O’Shea and Lemke 2014) replacing the viral plant-sounds study; denser register; new distractor set without the 'first to show' and reversal tells.

items.passage: The metallic-blue fruit of Pollia condensata, an herb of African forest understories, contains no blue pigment that can be extracted by conventional means. Examining the fruit’s outer cell walls, Silvia Vignolini et al. found multilayered stacks of cellulose microfibrils, arranged in a helicoidal pattern, that reflect light of particular wavelengths. Because layer thickness differs from cell to cell, the surface appears finely pixelated, and a specimen collected in Ghana in 1974 remains vividly colored. The researchers propose that such a fruit, dry and nutritionally unrewarding, may mimic a fleshy one, attracting seed dispersers without the metabolic cost of producing pulp.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Research suggests that Pollia condensata fruits owe their lasting color to cell-wall structure rather than pigment, which may help the plant attract seed dispersers without feeding them.
Vignolini et al. found that the blue pigment in Pollia condensata fruits resists decay unusually well, which explains why a specimen collected in Ghana decades ago remains brightly colored.
Research suggests that animals that disperse seeds prefer Pollia condensata fruits to the fleshy fruits of nearby understory plants because the fruits’ color is more intense.
Although Pollia condensata fruits reflect light strongly, the variation in layer thickness among cells makes their color too irregular for seed dispersers to notice.
items.explanation: The text says the fruit has no extractable blue pigment, that stacked cellulose layers in its cell walls reflect the light, and that the color lasts for decades; it then gives the researchers’ proposal that such a dry fruit may attract seed dispersers without the cost of pulp. Choice A joins the mechanism and the proposed benefit, keeping the text’s hedge (“may”).

B.why_wrong: The text says the fruit contains no extractable blue pigment; its color comes from the layered cell walls, not from a decay-resistant pigment.

C.why_wrong: The text never compares how seed dispersers respond to Pollia condensata and to other understory fruits; it only reports the researchers’ proposal that the fruit may mimic a fleshy one.

D.why_wrong: The text presents the pixelated surface as a feature of a vivid color and reports the proposal that the color attracts seed dispersers; nothing says the color is too irregular for them to notice.

sources.what: Vignolini et al. 2012, PNAS 109(39):15712-15715: P. condensata, African forest understory species; no blue pigment extractable by conventional means; color from Bragg reflection of helicoidally stacked cellulose microfibrils forming multilayers in epicarp cell walls; color differs cell to cell as layer thickness varies (pixelated, pointillist); dry fruit; specimen collected in Ghana in 1974 kept its strong color; fruits may mimic nutritious fruit to mislead seed dispersers without a nutritious reward, avoiding the energy cost of producing pulp
DOI of the paper

items.notes: New subject (replaces the peak-end colonoscopy study). Hard-tier 'et al.' naming as in 3.7, 3.9 and 3.21. The mimicry proposal is stated in the paper for structurally colored fruits and applied to Pollia; the passage keeps it hedged (propose, may).
items.replaced: IKEA effect, Norton, Mochon and Ariely (duplicate of inferences.S1.easy)
items.rewrite: New subject (Pollia condensata structural color, Vignolini et al. 2012) replacing the textbook peak-end colonoscopy study; dropped the 'one might expect... however' frame; denser register; key now the longest option.

items.passage: Histories of science have often cast scholars of the medieval Islamic world as custodians who translated Greek texts and passed them on to Renaissance Europe largely unaltered. Historian George Saliba has challenged that portrayal. He documents how astronomers writing in Arabic identified problems in Ptolemy’s account of planetary motion and proposed new models to resolve them. A geometric device introduced by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi in the thirteenth century and the planetary models of Ibn al-Shatir of Damascus in the fourteenth both closely resemble constructions that Copernicus used centuries later.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Saliba argues that Copernicus concealed how much his work owed to astronomers who wrote in Arabic.
Saliba shows that Arabic translations of Greek astronomy were less faithful to their sources than historians had assumed.
Al-Tusi and Ibn al-Shatir used new observations to confirm that Ptolemy’s account of planetary motion was accurate.
Saliba’s research indicates that astronomers in the medieval Islamic world did original work rather than merely preserving Greek science.
items.explanation: The text opens with the view that scholars in the medieval Islamic world mainly translated and passed on Greek texts, then says Saliba challenges it: astronomers writing in Arabic found problems in Ptolemy and proposed new models, some of which resemble ones Copernicus later used. Choice D states that correction.

A.why_wrong: The text says only that the earlier models resemble constructions Copernicus used; it says nothing about Copernicus concealing a debt.

B.why_wrong: Saliba challenges the idea that these scholars only translated, not the accuracy of their translations; the text never evaluates how faithful the translations were.

C.why_wrong: The text says the astronomers identified problems in Ptolemy’s account and proposed new models to resolve them, not that they confirmed it was accurate.

sources.what: Saliba, Islamic Science and the Making of the European Renaissance (MIT Press 2007): challenges the myths that Islamic science only carried forward Greek ideas and that modern science was created in Renaissance Europe; scholars recognized problems with Ptolemy; similarities between a model of al-Tusi (d. 1274) and those of Copernicus; Copernicus used Ibn al-Shatir’s models

Saliba: Professor of Arabic and Islamic Science at Columbia; mathematical models alternative to Ptolemy; Maragha tools (al-Tusi couple, Ibn al-Shatir model) found in the work of Copernicus; book published 2007
Ibn al-Shatir (1304-1375), astronomer in Damascus; his lunar and planetary models are mathematically similar to Copernicus’s
Tusi couple, geometric device introduced by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi in 1247/1260-61, later used by Copernicus

items.notes: New subject (replaces the medieval flat-Earth myth). The earlier view is the scholarly narrative Saliba targets, not a popular myth. “Closely resemble” keeps to the documented similarity; the passage does not claim that Copernicus borrowed directly, which is debated.
items.rewrite: New subject (George Saliba on astronomy in the medieval Islamic world) replacing the flat-Earth myth-debunking item; scholarly view-then-correction; new distractors; denser register; key is the longest option.

items.passage: A long-standing account holds that Spaniards in the Americas found Mesoamerican chocolate beverages unpalatable and accepted them only after removing unfamiliar spices and adding sugar, thereby adapting the drink to tastes they already had. Historian Marcy Norton contends that the evidence supports nearly the reverse. As cultural minorities in colonial Mesoamerica, Spaniards acquired a taste for chocolate on Indigenous terms, prizing its foam, its red coloring, and spices such as vanilla. The modifications that followed in Europe, she argues, were gradual responses to the technological and economic constraints of long-distance trade rather than a break with Mesoamerican preferences.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Norton argues that Spaniards stopped drinking chocolate as Mesoamericans prepared it once sugar became available, since sweetened drinks better suited their established tastes.
Norton argues that instead of adapting chocolate to their existing tastes, Spaniards in Mesoamerica adopted Indigenous preferences for it, and the drink changed only gradually thereafter.
Norton shows that chocolate gained acceptance in Europe chiefly because physicians recommended it as a medicine, which led Spaniards to overlook its unfamiliar flavor.
Although Spaniards in colonial Mesoamerica came to enjoy chocolate as it was prepared there, Norton argues, the drink they consumed in Europe soon bore little resemblance to the original.
items.explanation: The text sets out the long-standing account (Spaniards remade chocolate to suit tastes they already had) and then Norton’s reversal: Spaniards acquired a taste for chocolate on Indigenous terms, and later European changes were gradual adjustments rather than a break. Choice B carries both parts of her argument.

A.recipe: contradicts the text (affirms the earlier view)
A.why_wrong: This restates the long-standing account that Norton rejects; she argues that Spaniards adopted Indigenous preferences rather than abandoning them for sweetened drinks.

C.why_wrong: The text never mentions physicians or medicine; Norton explains Spaniards’ taste for chocolate by their position as cultural minorities in Mesoamerica.

D.recipe: twisted detail (half right, second half contradicted)
D.why_wrong: The first half fits the text, but Norton argues that the changes in Europe were gradual and did not break with Mesoamerican preferences, so the drink did not soon bear little resemblance to the original.

sources.what: Norton, “Tasting Empire: Chocolate and the European Internalization of Mesoamerican Aesthetics,” American Historical Review 111(3), 2006, 660-691 (English abstract printed with the Spanish translation): previous studies suggested Europeans transformed chocolate to fit their existing tastes; Norton shows Europeans learned to like chocolate on Indian terms as a result of their status as cultural minorities in colonial Mesoamerica

Same article (Spanish translation, p. 43): the myth that Spaniards found Indigenous chocolate distasteful and “corrected the bad taste” by eliminating New World spices and adding sugar; instead Europeans acquired a taste for Indigenous chocolate (appetite for spices such as vanilla, for the red color and for the foam); its composition evolved gradually through the technological and economic challenges of long-distance trade, not a radical break in aesthetic preferences
Norton, historian (University of Pennsylvania; earlier George Washington University); book Sacred Gifts, Profane Pleasures (Cornell, 2008)

items.notes: New subject (replaces “Let them eat cake”). The earlier view is a scholarly account Norton argues against, not a popular myth. The passage keeps to the article’s own list of valued features (foam, red color, spices such as vanilla). Hard two-part key, as in 3.4 and 3.21; distractor D is a two-part option with one wrong half.
items.replaced: painted ancient sculpture, Brinkmann and Koch-Brinkmann (duplicate of cross_text_connections.S1_solution.hard)
items.rewrite: New subject (Marcy Norton on how Spaniards acquired a taste for chocolate, AHR 2006) replacing the myth-debunking Marie Antoinette item; dropped the superlative distractor; two-part key that is the longest option.

items.passage: In 1990, filmmaker Zacharias Kunuk and his collaborators founded Igloolik Isuma Productions in Igloolik, an Arctic community in present-day Nunavut, Canada. The first production company in Canada majority-owned by Inuit, Isuma set out to preserve Inuit culture and language and to create jobs in Igloolik. Its productions, such as the television series Nunavut (Our Land), feature local residents recreating traditional life in the region. Its feature film Atanarjuat: The Fast Runner (2001) was the first ever written, directed, and acted entirely in Inuktitut.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Isuma was founded to keep Inuit language and traditions alive through filmmaking while also creating jobs in Igloolik.
Kunuk’s films have encouraged many young people in Igloolik to become professional actors.
Isuma’s productions show how life in Igloolik has changed since Nunavut became a territory.
Isuma’s films are made in Inuktitut because few people in Igloolik speak English.
items.explanation: The text states Isuma’s two aims (preserving Inuit culture and language, creating jobs in Igloolik) and then gives examples of how its work serves them: local residents recreating traditional life and a feature film made entirely in Inuktitut. Choice A sums up these aims and the means.

B.why_wrong: The text says local residents appear in Isuma’s productions, but it says nothing about young people going on to become professional actors.

C.why_wrong: The productions recreate traditional life in the region; the text does not say they depict changes in Igloolik since Nunavut became a territory.

D.why_wrong: The text links the use of Inuktitut to Isuma’s aim of preserving Inuit language; it says nothing about how many people in Igloolik speak English.

sources.what: Isuma: co-founded by Zacharias Kunuk, Paul Apak Angilirq and Norman Cohn in Igloolik in 1990; first Inuit-owned (75%) production company in Canada; aims to preserve Inuit culture and language and create jobs and economic development in Igloolik and Nunavut; local actors recreating Inuit life in the Igloolik region; 13-part series Nunavut (Our Land) 1994-95; Atanarjuat: The Fast Runner (2001) first feature film written, directed and acted entirely in Inuktitut
Kunuk biography: president and co-founder of Igloolik Isuma Productions; Atanarjuat won the Camera d’Or at Cannes 2001
Isuma’s own page on Kunuk
Nunavut became a territory in 1999 (hence “what is now Nunavut” for 1990)

items.notes: New subject (replaces Wangari Maathai and the Green Belt Movement). Some sources give 1988 for the start of Kunuk’s collaboration; the company’s founding as Igloolik Isuma Productions is usually dated 1990. “Collaborators” avoids the disputed list of co-founders. Distractors avoid the earlier set’s ‘mainly to’, ‘most widely admired’ and invented-earlier-practice recipes.

fixes: Lighter easy-tier register (“employment” to “jobs”, “in what is now” to “in present-day”, “recreating” as in the source)

items.rewrite: New subject (Zacharias Kunuk and Igloolik Isuma Productions) replacing the famous Green Belt Movement profile; new distractor recipes (invented effect, twisted detail, invented motive); key is the longest option.

items.passage: Oglala Lakota chef Sean Sherman, raised on the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota, constructs his menus around ingredients available in North America before European colonization. To reconstruct precolonial cuisine, he interviewed older community members and searched archives for descriptions of traditional Lakota foods. Owamni, the Minneapolis restaurant he opened in 2021, excludes wheat flour, dairy, cane sugar, beef, pork, and chicken, relying instead on bison, lake fish, and foraged plants. Yet Sherman insists that he is not trying to cook as people did in 1491; his aim is to adapt that knowledge for contemporary diners.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Sherman recreates specific Lakota meals described in historical archives as exactly as he can.
Sherman’s research shows that traditional Lakota foods were healthier than the foods introduced by European colonizers.
Sherman cooks with ingredients that predate European colonization but uses them to create food for people today.
Sherman opened Owamni so that older members of his community could taste the foods they remembered from childhood.
items.explanation: The text describes Sherman’s reliance on precolonial ingredients (his research and Owamni’s menu) and then adds, with “Yet,” that he aims to adapt that knowledge for contemporary diners rather than cook as people did in 1491. Choice C joins both halves.

A.why_wrong: The last sentence says Sherman is not trying to cook as people did in 1491; he adapts the knowledge rather than recreating archival meals exactly.

B.why_wrong: The text never compares the healthfulness of traditional Lakota foods and introduced foods; it describes only which ingredients Sherman uses and avoids.

D.why_wrong: Older community members appear in the text as sources Sherman interviewed, not as the people Owamni was opened to serve; the text says his food is meant for contemporary diners.

sources.what: Sherman: Oglala Lakota, grew up on the Pine Ridge reservation in South Dakota; interviewed older community members and searched archives for descriptions of traditional Lakota foods; founded The Sioux Chef 2014; Owamni in Minneapolis 2021, James Beard Best New Restaurant 2022; aim to take knowledge from the past and evolve it for today
Owamni excludes dairy, wheat flour, cane sugar, beef, pork and chicken; not cooking like it is 1491
Ingredients originally from the land: bison, rabbit, fish from the lake, wild plants; “We’re not trying to cook like it’s 1491”
Owamni made without flour, dairy, cane sugar, pork or other ingredients introduced after Europeans arrived

items.notes: New subject (replaces Kéré’s school in Gando). The main idea joins the precolonial ingredients with the turn in the last sentence, as the medium profile keys generalize. Distractors avoid the earlier set’s ‘mainly to show’, ‘most influential’ and invented-earlier-practice recipes.
items.rewrite: New subject (chef Sean Sherman and Owamni) replacing the Kéré profile; two-part key built on the passage’s turn; new distractor recipes (contradiction, invented comparison, invented motive); denser register.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Edmondo De Amicis’s 1886 novel Cuore (translated by Isabel F. Hapgood in 1887). Enrico, a schoolboy in Turin, Italy, is starting a new school year.

The school seemed to me so small and gloomy when I thought of the woods and the mountains where I had passed the summer! I thought again, too, of my master in the second class, who was so good, and who always smiled at us, and was so small that he seemed to be one of us, and I grieved that I should no longer see him there, with his tumbled red hair. I said to myself: “This is my first day. There are nine months more. What toil, what monthly examinations, what fatigue!”
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Enrico is excited to begin school again because he has missed his classmates over the summer.
Enrico is worried that he will do poorly on his examinations because he did not study during the summer.
Enrico wishes he could spend the school year in the mountains with his former master.
Enrico feels gloomy about the new school year, missing both his summer and his old teacher.
items.explanation: Enrico finds the school “small and gloomy” compared with the woods and mountains of his summer, grieves that he will no longer see his kind former master, and dreads the “nine months more” of toil ahead. Choice D sums up this unhappy mood and its two causes.

A.why_wrong: Enrico is unhappy, not excited: the school seems gloomy to him and he dreads the months ahead. He never mentions missing his classmates.

B.why_wrong: Enrico mentions monthly examinations only as part of the toil ahead; nothing suggests he failed to study over the summer or expects to do poorly.

C.why_wrong: The mountains are where Enrico spent his summer and the master is his teacher from the previous class; he misses each separately and never imagines spending the year in the mountains with the master.

sources.what: Text of Cuore (Heart): An Italian Schoolboy’s Journal, translated by Isabel F. Hapgood (Crowell; copyright 1887, 1895, 1901, 1915), chapter “The First Day of School”; passage copied exactly, with one sentence describing the new teacher omitted
Cuore, novel by Edmondo De Amicis published in 1886; journal of a schoolboy, Enrico, in Turin
Crowell edition of Hapgood’s translation, title page and copyright “1887 and 1895” by Thomas Y. Crowell & Company; excerpt text identical to the 1915 printing on Gutenberg

items.notes: New work (replaces the opening of The Wind in the Willows). De Amicis and Cuore appear in no official item of any skill and no other item in satbank/rw (grep). Adapted: the sentence describing the new teacher, between the second and third sentences, is omitted; straight quotation marks made curly. Source line gives the translation year as official items do (Heidi: “translated by Elisabeth Stork in 1915”): Hapgood’s translation was first copyrighted by Crowell in 1887; the 1915 notice in the Gutenberg text is Hapgood’s own copyright renewal, and the excerpt reads the same in the 1895 printing.

fixes: Source line now gives the translation year, as official items crediting translated works do: “(translated by Isabel F. Hapgood in 1887)” (Crowell copyright 1887)

items.rewrite: New work (Cuore, Hapgood translation) replacing the famous opening of The Wind in the Willows; new distractors without the damaged-house misreading.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from José Rizal’s 1887 novel Noli Me Tangere (translated by Charles Derbyshire in 1912). Sisa, a poor woman whose husband neglects the family, has spent the day preparing a special meal of rice, fish, tomatoes, and meat for her two young sons, who are coming home that night.

But by an unfortunate chance her husband came and ate the rice, the slices of wild boar’s meat, the duck leg, five of the little fishes, and the tomatoes. Sisa said nothing, although she felt as if she herself were being eaten. His hunger at length appeased, he remembered to ask for the boys. Then Sisa smiled happily and resolved that she would not eat that night, because what remained was not enough for three. The father had asked for their sons and that for her was better than eating.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Sisa happily goes without supper so that her sons can eat, finding her husband’s interest in them better than food.
Sisa is angry that her husband ate the meal but hides her feelings so that her sons will not be upset.
Sisa decides not to eat that night because she expects her sons to bring food home with them.
Sisa regrets having cooked such an elaborate meal, since her husband ate most of it before the boys came home.
items.explanation: After her husband eats most of the meal meant for the boys, Sisa is hurt but says nothing; when he asks about the boys, she smiles “happily,” decides not to eat so the remaining food can go to her sons, and finds his asking “better than eating.” Choice A captures both her sacrifice and the reason she is content.

B.why_wrong: Sisa feels hurt (“as if she herself were being eaten”), but the text then shows her smiling happily; nothing suggests anger or that she is shielding her sons, who are not yet home.

C.why_wrong: Sisa skips her meal because what remains “was not enough for three,” so she is saving it for her sons, not expecting them to bring food.

D.why_wrong: The husband does eat most of the meal, but the text never says Sisa regrets cooking it; her response is to give up her own share.

sources.what: Text of The Social Cancer: A Complete English Version of Noli Me Tangere, translated by Charles Derbyshire (1912), chapter XVI “Sisa”; sentences copied exactly (apostrophes curled)
Noli Me Tangere, novel by José Rizal published in 1887; Derbyshire’s English translation The Social Cancer, 1912

items.notes: New work (replaces Three Men in a Boat). Rizal appears in no official item of any skill and no other item in satbank/rw (grep). The excerpt is the closing paragraph of the scene, unchanged; the context sentence summarizes the preceding paragraph (Sisa prepared rice, small fish, tomatoes, wild boar meat and a duck leg for Basilio and Crispin). Sisa’s husband is described in the chapter as a heartless gambler.
items.rewrite: New work (Rizal’s Noli Me Tangere, Derbyshire translation) replacing the famous comic classic Three Men in a Boat; distractors without the fabricated-detail (medical student) tell; key is the longest option.

items.passage:
The following text is from Celia Thaxter’s 1861 poem “Land-Locked.” Thaxter grew up on the Isles of Shoals, islands off the coast of New Hampshire and Maine, and wrote the poem after moving to the mainland.

Black lie the hills, swiftly doth daylight flee,
And catching gleams of sunset’s dying smile,
Through the dusk land for many a changing mile
The river runneth softly to the sea.

O happy river, could I follow thee!
O yearning heart, that never can be still!
O wistful eyes, that watch the steadfast hill,
Longing for level line of solemn sea,

Have patience,—here are flowers and songs of birds,
Beauty and fragrance, wealth of sound and sight,
All summer’s glory thine from morn till night,
And life too full of joy for uttered words.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The speaker celebrates the arrival of summer, which has filled the countryside with flowers and birdsong.
The speaker longs to be near the sea despite trying to appreciate the summer beauty of the land.
The speaker plans to follow the river to the sea as soon as the summer has ended.
The speaker is saddened that the river carries the beauty of the hills away to the sea.
items.explanation: The speaker envies the river that reaches the sea (“could I follow thee!”), describes a “yearning heart” and eyes “Longing for level line of solemn sea,” and then urges patience by listing the flowers, birdsong and “summer’s glory” nearby. Choice B captures both the longing and the effort to be content.

A.why_wrong: The third stanza lists summer’s beauty only as a reason for “patience”; the poem’s central feeling is a yearning for the sea, not a celebration of summer.

C.why_wrong: “Could I follow thee!” is a wish, not a plan; the speaker never announces a plan to follow the river or mentions the end of summer.

D.why_wrong: The speaker calls the river “happy” because it reaches the sea; nothing suggests that it carries away the beauty of the hills or that this causes sadness.

sources.what: Text of “Land-locked,” stanzas 1-3, from Thaxter’s Poems (Hurd and Houghton), transcribed from the page scans on Wikisource; copied exactly (apostrophes curled)
Thaxter grew up on the Isles of Shoals (off New Hampshire); “Land-Locked,” her first published poem, was written on the mainland after her marriage and published in the Atlantic Monthly in 1861
Isles of Shoals straddle the border of Maine and New Hampshire

items.notes: New work (replaces Frost’s “A Time to Talk”). Thaxter appears in no official item of any skill and no other item in satbank/rw (grep). The excerpt is the first three of the poem’s six stanzas, unchanged except for curled apostrophes; the 1872 Poems text is used (the later collected edition changes some punctuation). Distractor C is a literal reading of a wish, not a restatement of lines.

fixes: Context line corrected: the Isles of Shoals lie off New Hampshire and Maine (they straddle the state border)

items.rewrite: New work (Celia Thaxter’s “Land-Locked”) replacing Frost’s well-known “A Time to Talk”; distractors are plausible misreadings rather than a literal restatement of negated lines.

items.passage:
The following text is Lizette Woodworth Reese’s 1899 poem “Tears.” The ancient Greek poet Homer was traditionally said to be blind, and in the Bible, King David mourns the death of his infant son.

When I consider Life and its few years—
A wisp of fog betwixt us and the sun;
A call to battle, and the battle done
Ere the last echo dies within our ears;
A rose choked in the grass; an hour of fears;
The gusts that past a darkening shore do beat;
The burst of music down an unlistening street,—
I wonder at the idleness of tears.
Ye old, old dead, and ye of yesternight,
Chieftains, and bards, and keepers of the sheep,
By every cup of sorrow that you had,
Loose me from tears, and make me see aright
How each hath back what once he stayed to weep:
Homer his sight, David his little lad!
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The speaker laments that even celebrated figures such as Homer and David endured losses that no achievement could repair.
The speaker suggests that the sorrows endured by people in ancient times were greater than those of the recently dead.
Because life is brief and the dead have regained what they once grieved for, the speaker regards weeping as pointless and asks to be freed from it.
Although the speaker at first considers tears useless, recalling the grief of Homer and David convinces the speaker that sorrow gives life meaning.
items.explanation: The first eight lines list images of life’s brevity (a wisp of fog, a battle over before its echo dies) and conclude “I wonder at the idleness of tears.” The last six lines ask the dead to “Loose me from tears” and to show the speaker that each has “back what once he stayed to weep,” as Homer has his sight and David his son. Choice C joins both parts of this reasoning.

A.recipe: literal or tonal misreading (reverses the ending)
A.why_wrong: The poem says Homer and David now have back what they lost (“Homer his sight, David his little lad!”); it does not lament losses that could not be repaired.

B.why_wrong: The speaker addresses both the “old, old dead” and those “of yesternight” together and never compares how much each group suffered.

D.why_wrong: The speaker does not change position; the mention of Homer and David supports the claim that tears are idle, and the speaker asks to be freed from them.

sources.what: Text of “Tears” as printed in Jessie B. Rittenhouse’s anthology The Little Book of Modern Verse (Project Gutenberg); spaced double hyphens set as closed em dashes
Reese’s sonnet “Tears” was published in Scribner’s Magazine in 1899
Tradition that Homer was blind
2 Samuel 12: the death of David’s infant son and David’s mourning
Second transcription of “Tears” confirming wording and punctuation

items.notes: New work (replaces Herbert’s much-anthologized “Virtue”). Reese appears in no official item of any skill and no other item in satbank/rw (grep). Whole sonnet, 14 lines, about 112 words of verse: above the poem median but within the skill maximum (116). The glosses on Homer and David go in the source line, as CB does for 3.17. Hard tier: the key must join the octave (life is brief, tears are idle) with the sestet (the dead have regained what they lost).
items.rewrite: New work (Lizette Woodworth Reese’s sonnet “Tears”) replacing Herbert’s canonical “Virtue”; no flat literal-misreading distractor; key is the longest option, carrying both halves of the argument.

items.passage: Classic Maya workers at the Paynes Creek Salt Works, on Belize’s southern coast, produced salt by boiling brine in ceramic vessels, and inland cities obtained the salt through trade. After rising seas submerged the site, acidic mangrove peat preserved wooden building posts but not bones, leaving little direct evidence of fish processing. When archaeologists Heather McKillop and Kazuo Aoyama examined excavated stone tools under a microscope, however, they found that most showed wear from cutting fish or meat. They concluded that salting fish, which could then be stored and transported, was a significant activity at the site.
items.stem: According to the text, what did McKillop and Aoyama conclude from their study of the stone tools?
options: Most of the stone tools were used to build the wooden structures at the site.
The salt works were abandoned because rising seas flooded the site.
Salt was produced at the site by boiling brine in ceramic vessels.
Salting fish, as well as making salt, was an important activity at the site.
items.explanation: The text says the tools showed wear from cutting fish or meat and that McKillop and Aoyama “concluded that salting fish ... was a significant activity at the site.” Choice D restates that conclusion.

A.why_wrong: The text says most of the tools showed wear from cutting fish or meat; nothing suggests they were used mainly for building.

B.why_wrong: The text says only that rising seas later submerged the site; it gives no reason the salt works were abandoned, and this was not something the researchers concluded from the tools.

C.why_wrong: The text does say salt was made by boiling brine in ceramic vessels, but that is background about the site, not what McKillop and Aoyama concluded from the stone tools.

sources.what: McKillop and Aoyama 2018, PNAS 115(43):10948-10952: Late to Terminal Classic chert tools from the Paynes Creek Salt Works, Belize; microscopic use-wear shows most tools used for cutting fish or meat; salting fish a significant activity; salted fish and salt cakes could be stored and traded; salt made by boiling brine in pots over fires; salt transported inland to Classic Maya cities; after abandonment the salt works were flooded by sea-level rise recorded in red mangrove peat, which preserved wooden building posts; the acidic peat would not have preserved fish or other bones
McKillop and Aoyama affiliations (LSU; Ibaraki University) and abstract via Europe PMC
McKillop 2005, PNAS: Late Classic saltworks in Punta Ycacos Lagoon, south coast of Belize, producing surplus salt largely for inland Maya cities

items.notes: New subject (replaces the Antikythera mechanism). “Classic Maya” follows the paper (Late to Terminal Classic, AD 600-900). The tool study is the 2018 PNAS paper; the background on salt making and inland trade comes from the same paper and McKillop 2005. Verification pass: the bones clause now follows the paper (the acidic peat would not have preserved fish or other bones; fish remains are virtually absent), and “therefore” was avoided because the tool study was not prompted by the missing bones (its fish-cutting result was unexpected).

fixes: “dissolved any skeletal remains” overstated the source; now “preserved wooden building posts but not bones, leaving little direct evidence of fish processing” (PNAS 2018)
Simplified prose made dense on purpose (“microscopically examined ... exhibited wear”)
All four options began with the same long prefix “Workers at the site”; options rewritten with varied openings, key echoing the conclusion as easy explicit-detail keys do
Distractor C now matches the passage’s “boiling brine”

items.rewrite: New subject (Maya salt works and fish salting, McKillop and Aoyama 2018) replacing the famous Antikythera mechanism; parallel options with a true-but-not-the-answer distractor instead of throwaway ones; denser register.

items.passage: Awe, the emotion elicited by encountering something vast that one cannot immediately comprehend, is thought to reduce self-focus by fostering what psychologists call a “small self.” To determine whether awe can be deliberately cultivated, neuroscientist Virginia Sturm and colleagues asked sixty healthy adults aged 60 to 90 to take a fifteen-minute outdoor walk every week for eight weeks; those randomly assigned to an “awe walk” group were instructed to seek out sources of wonder along the way. Participants photographed themselves during each walk. As the study progressed, those in the awe group occupied a diminishing portion of their photographs, leaving more room for the surrounding scenery, and their smiles became increasingly intense.
items.stem: What does the text indicate about the photographs taken by participants in the awe group?
options: Over time, the participants filled less of each image, and the surrounding scenery filled more.
They showed that these participants walked in a wider variety of locations than the other participants did.
They were used by the researchers to decide which participants should seek out sources of wonder.
They revealed that the participants smiled less as they paid more attention to their surroundings.
items.explanation: The last sentence says that as the study went on, participants in the awe group “occupied a diminishing portion of their photographs, leaving more room for the surrounding scenery.” Choice A restates this.

B.why_wrong: The text never says where either group walked or compares the variety of their routes; the photographs are described only in terms of how much space the participants and the scenery took up and how the participants smiled.

C.recipe: twisted detail (wrong role in the method)
C.why_wrong: The text says participants were randomly assigned to the awe walk group, which was instructed to seek out sources of wonder; the photographs were a record taken during the walks, not a basis for that assignment.

D.why_wrong: The text says the awe group’s smiles “became increasingly intense,” not that they smiled less.

sources.what: Sturm et al. 2020/2022, Emotion, “Big Smile, Small Self: Awe Walks Promote Prosocial Positive Emotions in Older Adults”: awe defined as emotion in the presence of vast things not immediately understood, reduces self-focus, “small self”; sixty healthy older participants aged 60 to 90 (UCSF); weekly 15-minute outdoor walks for eight weeks; random assignment to awe walk or control walk; awe group taught to orient walks to experience wonder; participants photographed themselves on each walk; awe walkers showed an increasingly small self in their photographs (less of themselves, more background scenery) and increasing smile intensity
DOI of the paper
Sturm, PhD, associate professor of neurology and psychiatry at UCSF who leads the Clinical Affective Neuroscience lab; random assignment to the awe walk group

items.notes: New subject (replaces the marshmallow-test replication). Sturm is in the UCSF Department of Neurology. The passage says only that some participants were randomly assigned to the awe walk group (52 were analyzed, 24 awe and 28 control), so it gives no group sizes.

fixes: “neurologist” was wrong for Sturm (a PhD who leads a clinical affective neuroscience lab): now “neuroscientist”
“half were instructed” replaced by the paper’s random assignment to an “awe walk” group (group sizes were not equal)

items.rewrite: New subject (awe walks and self-photographs, Sturm et al. 2020) replacing the textbook marshmallow-test replication; new stem frame (What does the text indicate about X?); denser register.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Benito Pérez Galdós’s 1878 novel Marianela (translated by Clara Bell in 1883). Teodoro Golfin, a doctor, is traveling on foot at night to the mines where his brother lives.

He presently stopped, and gazing round the dim horizon, he seemed vexed and puzzled. He evidently was not sure of his way and was looking round for some passing native of the district who might give him such topographical information as might enable him to reach his destination. “A pretty state of things!” he exclaimed, trying to console himself for this provoking situation by his sense of the ridiculous. “What have we here?... A stone; capital—a good seat while I smoke a cigar and wait for the moon to rise.” The philosophical Golfin seated himself as calmly as if it were a bench by a promenade.
items.stem: Based on the text, how does Golfin most likely respond to having lost his way?
options: He hurries back toward the town he passed earlier so that he can ask someone for directions.
He treats his predicament with humor and settles down to wait calmly.
He worries that he will not find shelter before the night grows cold.
He gives up on reaching the mines and decides to spend the night on the stone.
items.explanation: Although Golfin is at first “vexed and puzzled,” he tries to console himself “by his sense of the ridiculous,” jokes that a stone is “a good seat” while he smokes and waits for the moon, and sits down “as calmly as if it were a bench by a promenade.” Together these details show that he meets the situation with humor and calm (choice B).

A.why_wrong: Golfin does not hurry anywhere; he sits down on a stone to smoke and wait.

C.why_wrong: The text never mentions shelter or cold, and Golfin’s calm behavior does not suggest worry.

D.why_wrong: Golfin sits on the stone only to wait for the moon to rise; nothing suggests he abandons his journey for the night.

sources.what: Text of Marianela, “from the Spanish by Clara Bell” (New York: Gottsberger, 1883), chapter I “Gone Astray”; sentences copied exactly (straight quotes curled, double hyphen as em dash), with intervening sentences omitted
Marianela, novel by Benito Pérez Galdós written in 1878

items.notes: New work (replaces The Wonderful Wizard of Oz). Galdós and Marianela appear in no official item of any skill and no other item in satbank/rw (grep). Adapted by trimming: the excerpt joins sentences from the first pages of chapter I; Golfin’s quoted remark starts partway through a longer speech. Golfin is the doctor Teodoro Golfín (spelled without the accent in Bell’s translation), walking to the Socartes mines where his brother works. The final sentence is trimmed after “promenade” (the original continues “, and was preparing for his smoke, when he heard a voice ...”), an adaptation the “adapted from” line covers.
items.rewrite: New work (Galdós’s Marianela, Clara Bell translation) replacing the very famous Wizard of Oz excerpt; stem asks how the character responds, with plausible rather than silly distractors.

items.passage: Many animals are countershaded: darker on the back than on the belly, a pattern that offsets the shadows cast by overhead light and makes the body appear flatter to predators. Among hoofed mammals, species of open habitats, where direct sunlight predominates, typically show an abrupt transition from dark to light high on the body, whereas species living beneath forest canopies, where illumination is diffuse, show a smoother gradation. From fossilized pigment in an exceptionally preserved specimen of the dinosaur Psittacosaurus, paleontologist Jakob Vinther’s team reconstructed its coloration. The animal’s dark back graded smoothly into a pale underside relatively far down the body.
items.stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the habitat of the Psittacosaurus that Vinther’s team studied?
options: It was an open landscape where the dinosaur was exposed mainly to direct overhead sunlight.
It was shared with hoofed mammals whose coloring closely resembled that of the dinosaur.
It changed from forest to open grassland during the period in which the dinosaur lived.
It was a forest where light reached the ground diffusely through the canopy.
items.explanation: The text says that animals living under forest canopies, where light is diffuse, show a smooth gradation from dark to light, while animals of open, sunny habitats show an abrupt transition high on the body. The Psittacosaurus had a smooth gradation far down the body, so it most likely lived in a forest with diffuse light (choice D). The text never states this conclusion; it follows from the two descriptions together.

A.why_wrong: An open habitat with direct sunlight goes with an abrupt transition high on the body, which is the opposite of the pattern found on the Psittacosaurus.

B.why_wrong: The hoofed mammals are cited only as evidence of how countershading varies with light; the text never says they lived alongside the dinosaur or looked like it.

C.why_wrong: The text describes one specimen’s coloration and says nothing about the habitat changing over time.

sources.what: Vinther et al. 2016, Current Biology 26(18):2456-2462: countershading (dark dorsum, light ventrum) counteracts the gradient of overhead illumination, removing 3D shape cues; ungulate evidence: open habitats with direct overhead sun show a sharp dark-light transition high up the body, closed habitats (forest canopy, diffuse light) a smoother gradation; exceptionally preserved Psittacosaurus specimen from the Jehol biota with preserved melanin; gradation from dark to light relatively far down the body, matching diffuse illumination; conclusion that it inhabited a closed forest habitat
DOI of the paper

items.notes: New subject (replaces the coelacanth story). Vinther (University of Bristol) is a paleontologist who studies fossil color. The passage gives the two premises and leaves the forest conclusion, which is the paper's own, for the student to draw.

fixes: Removed the participial method opener (“Analyzing fossilized pigment ..., paleontologist ... and colleagues”) and the “and colleagues” frame shared with two other items; stem adjusted to “Vinther’s team”

items.rewrite: New subject (Psittacosaurus countershading and habitat, Vinther et al. 2016) replacing the textbook coelacanth story; real two-premise inference instead of a chronological narrative; denser register.

items.passage: In 1577 a questionnaire designed by Juan López de Velasco, chief cosmographer of Spain’s Council of the Indies, was sent to local officials in the Americas. López de Velasco intended to compile their answers into a comprehensive description of the Indies, and one question requested a map of each town depicting its streets, plazas, and other notable features. Many Spanish officials in New Spain, art historian Barbara Mundy has shown, wrote the textual answers themselves but delegated the maps to Indigenous painters. These painters represented their communities as pre-Hispanic manuscript painters had, using place-name glyphs, stylized trees, and trails of footprints to convey a community’s history and social order rather than its topography.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the maps that Indigenous painters made in response to the questionnaire?
options: They likely recorded distances between communities more precisely than the maps that Spanish officials drew themselves.
They likely led López de Velasco to send out a revised questionnaire asking officials to draw the maps themselves.
They were likely of limited use for the comprehensive description of the Indies that López de Velasco intended to compile.
They likely reflected Spanish officials’ instructions about which features of each community the painters should emphasize.
items.explanation: López de Velasco meant to compile the answers into a comprehensive description of the Indies and asked for a map of each town’s streets, plazas, and other features, but the Indigenous painters conveyed each community’s history and social order through glyphs, trees, and footprints rather than its topography. Together these suggest that the maps were poorly suited to his purpose (choice C). The text never says so directly.

A.why_wrong: The text says the Indigenous painters conveyed history and social order rather than topography, and it never compares their maps’ precision with maps drawn by Spanish officials.

B.why_wrong: The text says nothing about any revised questionnaire or about how López de Velasco responded to the maps.

D.why_wrong: The text says the officials delegated the maps and that the painters followed pre-Hispanic conventions instead of the questionnaire’s request; nothing indicates that officials directed what the painters emphasized.

sources.what: Review of Mundy, The Mapping of New Spain (Cartographic Perspectives 27, 1997): officials in charge (Esquivel, López de Velasco) assumed Spanish colonists would be the respondents and that responses might be collated to make the empire visible; settlers devoted their attention to the written responses and doled out the pictorial and cartographic work to native mapmakers, nearly always from the nobility; maps traced with iconic animals, stylized trees and trails of footprints; native mapmakers mapped the community as a history and social structure rather than topography; López de Velasco, discouraged by the syncretistic, non-arithmetic maps, set them aside

Philip II’s 1577 decree; Juan López de Velasco, cosmógrafo-cronista mayor of the Council of the Indies, designed the fifty-question inquiry; Mundy: 45 of 69 pinturas (65%) by Indigenous artists; the questionnaire was the Instrucción y memoria de las relaciones que se han de hacer para la descripción de las Indias
Mundy, The Mapping of New Spain: Indigenous Cartography and the Maps of the Relaciones Geográficas (University of Chicago Press, 1996)
Indigenous artists of the Relaciones maps; logographic place-names (Teozacoalco); Mundy: the maps best show the Indigenous world

The 1577 Instrucción y memoria de las relaciones que se han de hacer para la descripción de las Indias, designed by López de Velasco (cosmographer and chronicler of the Indies) to gather information on every town
One question of the questionnaire asked for a map (pintura) including the town’s center, streets, plazas, monasteries and other important features

items.notes: New subject (replaces Ashurbanipal’s tablets). The key is Mundy’s own conclusion (the maps were of little use to Spain’s cosmographers), left unstated so that it must be inferred from the purpose of the questionnaire and the painters’ conventions. “Many” officials reflects the reviewers’ “with some exceptions” and Mundy’s count (45 of 69 maps by Indigenous artists). Verification pass: the second sentence now states what the requested maps were to show (streets, plazas and other features), so the inference that the painters’ history-and-society maps were of limited use rests on stated premises; “rather than its topography” follows the review of Mundy (native mapmakers mapped the community rather than the topography).

fixes: Blind solve found the key’s link weak (the text never said what López de Velasco needed from the maps): passage now states that a question requested a map of each town’s streets, plazas, and other features, and the painters conveyed history and social order “rather than its topography”
Explanation and why_wrong for A and D updated

items.rewrite: New subject (Indigenous painters of the Relaciones Geográficas maps, Barbara Mundy) replacing the well-known Ashurbanipal fire story; compact two-premise inference instead of a fact dump; key is the longest option.

items.passage: Many plants synthesize caffeine as a chemical defense, since at high concentrations the compound is toxic to insects. Low doses nonetheless occur in the floral nectar of coffee and citrus plants, which benefit from bee pollination, and why such plants would put a defensive compound in their nectar has been unclear. A team led by neuroscientist Geraldine Wright found that honeybees rewarded with sugar solution containing nectar-level caffeine were three times as likely as bees rewarded with sugar alone to remember an associated floral scent a day later. Because nectar concentrations never exceed the threshold at which bees detect caffeine’s bitterness, the compound may promote pollinator fidelity without discouraging visits.
items.stem: Which question does the text most directly attempt to answer?
options: Why do some plants that benefit from bee pollination produce nectar containing caffeine?
How does the concentration of caffeine in coffee nectar compare with that in citrus nectar?
Which insects besides honeybees avoid flowers whose nectar contains caffeine?
Do coffee and citrus plants produce more seeds when they are pollinated by honeybees than by other insects?
items.explanation: The second sentence names the puzzle: why plants that benefit from bee pollination would put a defensive compound in their nectar. The rest of the text answers it: caffeine at nectar levels helps bees remember the flower’s scent at concentrations too low for them to detect its bitterness. Choice A restates that question.

B.why_wrong: The text says only that low doses occur in coffee and citrus nectar; it never compares the two plants’ concentrations.

C.why_wrong: The text discusses only honeybees and says nothing about which other insects avoid caffeinated nectar.

D.why_wrong: The text says only that these plants benefit from bee pollination; it never compares their seed production with honeybees and with other insects.

sources.what: Wright et al. 2013, Science 339(6124):1202-1204: plant drugs are toxic defenses against herbivores; caffeine toxic and repellent to honeybees at high concentrations; caffeine occurs at low doses in the nectar of Coffea and Citrus, which produce more fruit and seed when pollinated by bees; bees rewarded with nectar-level caffeine were three times as likely to remember a learned floral scent 24 h later; nectar caffeine never exceeded the bees’ bitter taste threshold; plants secure pollinator fidelity
Newcastle University press release naming Geraldine Wright as lead researcher; three times as likely to remember after 24 hours; dose too low for bees to taste
DOI of the paper

items.notes: New subject (replaces the zebra-stripe study). The question is posed indirectly (“why such plants would ... has been unclear”) rather than as a direct question, and then answered, as in 2.20. Wright was at Newcastle University’s Institute of Neuroscience.

fixes: “which depend on bees for pollination” overstated the paper (coffee and citrus produce more fruit and seed when bees pollinate them): now “which benefit from bee pollination”, with the key reworded to match
Deterrence clause now follows the paper’s bitter-taste threshold
Varied the “[role] [name] and colleagues” frame shared with two other items

items.rewrite: New subject (caffeine in nectar and bee memory, Wright et al. 2013) replacing the famous zebra-stripe study; question embedded indirectly instead of a rhetorical question; denser register; new distractor questions.
